extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, and readers of English common law (legal scholars/practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository legal treatise material describing the roles, rights, duties, methods of appointment, and modes of vacancy for ecclesiastical officers (bishops, deans, parsons, vicars, curates, churchwardens, parish clerks) and principal rules on creation/incidents of the nobility in English common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dean and chapter check on bishop's grants
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law, until statute 32 Hen. VIII. c. 28, a bishop's grant or lease would not bind his successors unless confirmed by the dean and chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical rule limiting bishop's power to bind successors; statutory change (32 Hen. VIII c. 28) modified this effect of grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voidance of deaneries and prebends
rubrics_metrics.description: Deaneries and prebends may become void by death, deprivation, or resignation to either the king or the bishop; if a dean, prebendary, or other spiritual person is made a bishop, all the preferments he was before possessed of are void (voidance occurs upon consecration, not election).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferments become void upon elevation to bishopric (consecration). Resignation must be to the proper superior (king or bishop) to produce voidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archdeacon jurisdiction and court
rubrics_metrics.description: An arch-deacon has ecclesiastical jurisdiction subordinate to the bishop, visits the clergy, and has a separate court for punishment by spiritual censures and for hearing ecclesiastical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archdeaconial authority is originally derived from the bishop but functions now as a distinct jurisdiction with visitation and a separate court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural deans' inferior inspection and judicial authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Rural deans are ancient deputies of the bishop who inspected parochial clergy and were armed with an inferior degree of judicial and coercive authority; though largely fallen into disuse, deaneries persist as ecclesiastical divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primarily historical/administrative office; powers vary by custom and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and rights of a parson (persona ecclesiae)
rubrics_metrics.description: A parson (persona ecclesiae) has full possession of all the rights of a parochial church, represents the church (is a body corporate), and has during life the freehold in the parsonage house, the glebe, the tithes, and other dues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal significance: parson 'personates' the church and holds rights to protect church property by perpetual succession; may also be called rector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of benefices (requirements and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A benefice may be 'appropriated' (annexed perpetually) to a spiritual corporation (e.g., monastery); to complete appropriation the king's licence and consent of the bishop must be obtained, and the patron's consent is necessarily implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: to prevent lapse and because law trusts king and bishop not to prejudice the church; appropriators become perpetual parsons and sue/be sued by the name of parsons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severance (disappropriation) of appropriated benefice
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation may be severed if the patron or appropriator presents a clerk who is instituted and inducted (the presented clerk becomes complete parson), or if the appropriating corporation is dissolved (common law disappropriation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once severed by proper institution & induction, appropriation cannot be re-united except by repeating those solemnities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicar as deputy and statutory endowment obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a church is appropriated, the appropriator deputes a minister called a 'vicar' whose stipend is at the appropriator's discretion, but statutes (15 Ric. II c. 6; 4 Hen. IV c. 12) require the bishop to ordain competent sums for poor parishioners and that the vicarage be 'sufficiently endowed' and that vicars be secular, perpetual, canonically instituted and inducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes were enacted to prevent scandalous neglect by appropriators: bishop must fix a pension for the poor and ensure sufficient vicarial endowment; vicars cannot be removable at monastery caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between parson and vicar
rubrics_metrics.description: The parson generally has the whole right to ecclesiastical dues in the parish; the vicar usually serves under an appropriator who takes the best part of profits and to whom the vicar is effectively a perpetual curate with a standing salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local variations exist: some vicarages have large shares of great tithes (augmentations made permanent by statute 29 Car. II c. 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites to become a parson or vicar
rubrics_metrics.description: Four requisites necessary: holy orders; presentation; institution; and induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution confers the spiritual part (care of souls); induction confers the temporal part (possession of parsonage/glebe/tithes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and ordination qualifications for benefices
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute 13 Eliz. c. 12 no person under twenty-three in deacon's orders should be presented to any benefice with cure, and if not ordained priest within one year after induction would be ipso facto deprived; by statute 13 & 14 Car. II c. 4 no person is capable to be admitted to any benefice unless first ordained priest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical statutory restrictions on age and required ordination status; common-law allowances (e.g., deacon instituted) were altered by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simony: forbidden conferment by money and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person obtains orders or a licence to preach by money or corrupt practices (simony), the person giving such orders forfeits 40_l., the person receiving 10_l., and the receiver is incapable of any ecclesiastical preferment for seven years (stat. 31 Eliz. c. 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simony renders subsequent preferment invalid and imposes monetary forfeitures and a period of incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds on which bishop may refuse a patron's presented clerk
rubrics_metrics.description: The bishop may refuse for several reasons: (1) if the patron is excommunicated and remains in contempt forty days; (2) if the clerk be 'unfit'—unfitness may be personal (bastard, outlaw, excommunicate, alien, under age), moral/faith defects (particular heresy or malum in se), or want of learning; general allegations (e.g., 'schismaticus inveteratus' or tavern-haunting) are not sufficient cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If refusal is for ecclesiastical (spiritual) causes the bishop must give notice to the patron; for temporal causes notice is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure on judicial challenge to bishop's refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: If patron brings an action against the bishop for refusing a clerk, the bishop must assign the cause: temporal causes may be decided by king's courts (judges or jury); spiritual causes when fact denied go to a jury, and if admitted/found the court consults learned divines to decide sufficiency; for 'minus sufficiens in literatura' the metropolitan reexamines and its certificate is final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different forums and fact-finding rules apply depending on whether the cause is temporal or spiritual; metropolitan certification final for learning insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution (spiritual investiture) effects and collation
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution is the investiture of the spiritual part of the benefice (care of souls). On institution a vicar may take an oath of perpetual residence (if required). When the ordinary is also the patron, presentation and institution are the same act called collation. By institution a clerk may enter parsonage house and take tithes but cannot grant/let or bring action for them until induction; the crown may revoke an instituted clerk before induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution fills the church spiritually; actual legal control over temporalities requires induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction (temporal investiture) formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is performed by a mandate from the bishop to the archdeacon (who issues precepts) and is effected by giving corporal possession of the church (holding the ring, tolling a bell, etc.) to give parishioners notice; induction is the investiture of the temporal part of the benefice and, together with presentation and institution, makes full possession ('persona impersonata').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremonial corporal acts are legally required to perfect the temporal investiture and notify parishioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residence duty and statutory penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute 21 Hen. VIII. c. 13 persons wilfully absenting themselves from their benefices for one month together, or two months in the year, incur a penalty of 5_l. to the king and 5_l. to any person that will sue, with enumerated exceptions (chaplains to the king, certain heads of houses, magistrates, university professors, bona fide students under 40). Legal residence includes residence in the parsonage house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residence requirement serves to ensure service, hospitality and house maintenance; failure exposes monetary penalties and private suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of ceasing to be parson or vicar
rubrics_metrics.description: A parson or vicar may cease by: (1) death; (2) cession (accepting another benefice) — stat. 21 Hen. VIII c.13 provides that accepting another benefice of 8_l. per annum or upwards in king's books adjudges the first void unless dispensed; (3) consecration (promotion to bishopric voids other preferments) though 'commenda' may allow holding in commendam; (4) resignation accepted by the ordinary; (5) deprivation by canonical censures or pursuant penal statutes (simony; maintaining doctrine derogatory to king's supremacy, 39 articles, or book of common-prayer; neglecting reading articles or taking oaths; using other form of prayer; other statutory cases) — in many such cases benefice is ipso facto void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dispensations and commenda are statutory/prerogative exceptions; many statutory causes create automatic vacancy without formal sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenda (holding benefice in commendam)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Commenda' or 'ecclesia commendata' is a living commended by the crown to the care of a clerk to hold till a proper pastor is provided; it may be temporary (one–three years) or perpetual and can function as a dispensation to avoid vacancy ('commenda retinere' or 'commenda recipere').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prerogative device allowing temporary/perpetual retention of a living; treated as a species of dispensation to avert vacancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curates: perpetual and temporary curacies and statutory stipend rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A curate is a lower degree minister; 'perpetual curacies' exist where all tithes are appropriated and no vicarage endowed (exempted from the statute of Hen. IV); statutes require that those serving during vacancy be paid such stipend as the ordinary thinks reasonable out of profits of the vacancy (or by successor within fourteen days); when a rector or vicar nominates a curate to be licenced the ordinary shall settle his stipend between 20_l. and 50_l. per annum and on failure of payment may sequester profits of the benefice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutory protections apply to curates to secure stipend during vacancies; ordinary has a role in fixing and enforcing stipend limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Churchwardens' powers and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Churchwardens are guardians/keepers of the church and representatives of the parish; they may be appointed by minister, parish, or both; they have, in some respects, corporate capacity at common law to hold goods and chattels and bring actions for parish benefit, may be removed by the parish and called to account, have duties to repair the church and to make rates/levies (recoverable only in ecclesiastical court), join overseers for poor relief, levy a shilling forfeiture on absentees from church on Sundays/holidays, and may keep order (e.g., removing a hat). They have no interest in real property (lands, churchyard) — actions for damage to real property belong to the parson or vicar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide array of petty parochial statutory powers; some remedies limited to ecclesiastical courts; removable by parish/custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish clerks and sextons as freeholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Parish clerks and sextons are regarded as persons who have freeholds in their offices and therefore cannot be deprived by ecclesiastical censures (though they may be punished); they are generally appointed by the incumbent but, where custom chooses them by inhabitants, a mandamus will be granted to the arch-deacon to swear them in to enforce custom as a temporal right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom that has become established may create a civil right enforceable by king's courts (mandamus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriator's duty to repair church and provide for service
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriators (corporations holding benefices) were bound to repair the church and provide for its constant supply; historically appropriations that deprived parishes of service led to statutes requiring pensions for the poor and sufficient endowment of vicarages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and statutory responses aimed to correct neglect by appropriators (e.g., 15 Ric. II c.6; 4 Hen. IV c.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of peers: writ versus patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers are created either by writ (summons to attend House of Peers) or by patent (royal grant). Creation by writ is ancient but ennoblement by writ requires the person actually to take his seat; creation by patent is the commoner, surer method and enures according to the limitations in the patent. A creation by writ holds to 'him and his heirs' without words; patents require words to direct inheritance or the dignity may enure only for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs: writ may confer inheritance to heirs without express words; patent gives express control over limitations but must include words of inheritance to pass beyond life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer incidents: trial by peers
rubrics_metrics.description: One incident of the nobility is that in criminal cases a nobleman shall be tried by his peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic common-law privilege of peers in criminal trial procedure.
